q: According to Percival Spear, the new urban middle class that emerged under British rule was characterised as:
o: A well-integrated all-India class with a common foreground of knowledge, ideas and values, and a sense of unity of purpose
A class entirely opposed to Western education
A regionally fragmented class with no shared values
A class limited exclusively to the landed aristocracy

q: Which of the following theories, put forward by European scholars during the rediscovery of India's past, gave a psychological boost to educated Indians?
o: That Indian society had always been static and unchanging
That India had no civilisation of its own before British contact
That ancient India lacked any form of trade with the outside world
That the Indo-Aryans belonged to the same ethnic group from which other European nations had evolved

q: The Ilbert Bill controversy arose when Lord Ripon's government attempted to:
o: Impose the Vernacular Press Act on Indian newspapers
Introduce separate electorates for Muslims
Abolish judicial disqualification based on race, giving Indian members of the covenanted civil service the same judicial powers as Europeans
Reduce the age limit for the Indian Civil Service examination

q: Which of the following best describes the nationalist lesson drawn from the Ilbert Bill episode?
o: It became clear that justice and fair play could not be expected where European interests were at stake, but the European agitation also taught nationalists methods of organised protest
It convinced nationalists that constitutional agitation was futile and should be abandoned
Indians concluded that racial equality had been fully achieved
It led directly to the repeal of the Vernacular Press Act

q: The Zamindari Association, popularly known as the 'Landholders' Society', primarily represented the interests of:
o: Muslim peasants of Bengal
Educated middle-class professionals
Landlords, and is considered the beginning of organised political activity and constitutional agitation in India
Industrial workers

q: Some of the British Indian Association's demands were partially met when the Charter Act of 1853 provided for:
o: Complete Indianisation of the civil services
Abolition of the East India Company altogether
Addition of six members to the governor-general's council for legislative purposes
Establishment of a fully elected Indian legislature

q: The Madras Mahajan Sabha, founded in 1884, was established by:
o: Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose
Badruddin Tyabji and Pherozshah Mehta
M. Viraraghavachari, B. Subramaniya Aiyer and P. Anandacharlu
Sisir Kumar Ghosh

q: The pre-Congress campaign 'in support of the Ilbert Bill' by Indian political associations reflected their support for:
o: Removing racial disqualification in the judiciary that denied Indian civil servants judicial powers over Europeans
Imposing tariffs on British manufactured imports
Restricting the entry of Christian missionaries into India
Reducing the salaries of higher British officials

q: Which of the following best explains why 'political, administrative and economic unification' of India under British rule aided the growth of nationalism, according to the chapter?
o: It eliminated all regional identities in favour of a single British identity
It had no bearing on the growth of nationalist sentiment
It ensured equal economic development across all regions of India
It linked the economic fate of different regions together and enabled modern transport/communication to bring leaders from different regions together for political mobilisation

q: Which of the following genuinely reflects the 'two-fold effect' of political and economic unification as identified by nationalists?
o: Complete elimination of famine across India, and creation of full political democracy
Total industrialisation of India, and equal wages for all workers
Linking regional economic fates together, and enabling exchange of political ideas among leaders from different regions via modern transport and communication
Universal literacy across India, and abolition of caste distinctions

q: According to the chapter, most political associations of the early 19th century, prior to those dominated by the educated middle class later in the century, were chiefly composed of:
o: Peasants and agricultural labourers
Religious clergy across all faiths
Industrial workers and trade unionists
Wealthy and aristocratic elements, often local or regional in character
